articles.title: A 1980 will left a historic merchant’s house to become a museum; a 2026 High Court ruling questioned whether the council had to preserve it under a trust
articles.summary: A 17th-century merchant’s house in Topsham, Exeter, has become the subject of a High Court ruling following a dispute over the wishes set out in its
articles.body: A 17th-century merchant’s house in Topsham, Exeter, has become the subject of a High Court ruling following a dispute over the wishes set out in its former owner’s 1980 will. Dorothy Holman left 25 The Strand to Exeter City Council so it could continue as a museum, having established one there in 1967. However, in a judgment handed down on 16 October 2026, the court ruled that the council owns the property beneficially and is not obliged to preserve it as a museum under a trust. The decision clarified the legal effect of Holman’s will and memorandum of wishes.How a 1980 will left the property to Exeter City CouncilThe property at 25 The Strand consists of a house and garden situated alongside the estuary of the River Exe in Topsham. According to the High Court judgment, the building was constructed in 1688, and part of it has been listed Grade II on the National Heritage List for England since 1952. Holman came from a family with a long history of involvement in merchant shipping and shipbuilding in Topsham. She reportedly purchased the property from her brother, Alwyn, in 1939 and died there in 1983, aged 95.Holman had already established a small museum in the property's sail loft in 1967. Its initial displays focused on her family's shipbuilding background, before expanding over the years. Under clause 4 of her will, she devised the freehold property to the council, subject to conditions set out in clause 10. These included a requirement that the council resolve, within six months of her death, to accept the property and confirm its intention to use it in accordance with a memorandum of wishes signed by her and found with the will.Why Holman wanted the property to remain a museum for TopshamHolman's accompanying memorandum explained why she wanted to give the property to the City and County of the City of Exeter. According to the document reproduced in the judgment, she wrote: "My object in giving my house and furniture to the City and County of the City of Exeter is to provide a place where members of the public interested in the history of Topsham can see both a museum of the town’s history and a typical Topsham merchant’s house of 1700–1870."She also expressed specific wishes concerning the building and its contents. Holman hoped that the furniture would remain in the house, that most of her pictures and all drawings and sculptures by her sister would be permanently displayed, and that the garden between the road and river would continue to be used as a garden rather than a car park. She also suggested that the museum could be expanded as more suitable material became available. Most importantly, she stated: "It is my wish that my home will always be the museum for Topsham. My gift is being made for no other purpose." If the house became unsuitable for use as a museum, she wished it to be sold and the proceeds used towards providing another museum within the parish of Topsham.However, the judge noted that the memorandum was signed by Holman but did not contain witnesses' signatures. It therefore did not comply with section 9 of the Wills Act 1837 and could not be treated as a testamentary document. The court considered its wording when examining the intention behind the will, but the memorandum's statements of hopes and wishes did not automatically create enforceable obligations.Exeter City Council accepts ownership of the historic Topsham museumFollowing Holman's death on 11 July 1983, probate was granted to the will's executors on 20 October that year. Exeter City Council accepted the property at a joint meeting of its Policy Committee and Leisure Committee on 22 November 1983, indicating its intention to use it in accordance with the memorandum. The full council received and adopted the meeting's minutes on 6 December 1983. The executors subsequently assented to the transfer on 16 July 1984, and the property was registered in the council's name.The Topsham Museum Society was formed by local residents to continue operating the museum. Its trustees obtained charitable registration in 1984, and the council granted them a six-year lease in April 1985. The museum reopened to the public in 1986. Further leases followed in 1991 and 1997, with the latter running for 30 years. In 2019, a new charitable incorporated organisation, Topsham Museum, was formed and registered as a charity. The remaining term of the 1997 lease was assigned to the organisation in February 2022.The dispute arose after the building required substantial repairs. In May 2024, the council commissioned work costing £106,000 to address problems with the render on the property's side elevation. After the old render was removed, additional structural repairs and upgrades were identified, increasing the estimated budget to approximately £430,000. The museum was temporarily closed in December 2024, and its artefacts were removed from the period-house section and placed in off-site storage. Work on the property stopped at the end of June 2025 after the original contract works were completed.By November 2025, the council had begun further work to make the premises watertight and allow scaffolding to be removed from the adjoining side street. However, the additional work required was estimated to cost another £500,000. The council said it could not meet the remaining costs from its existing budgets and would need to borrow to complete the repairs. Its legal position was important because, if it owned the property beneficially, it would have more options, including borrowing against the property or selling or leasing part or all of it on commercial terms.Why the court examined whether Holman's will created a legal trustExeter City Council issued its claim under Part 8 of the Civil Procedure Rules on 27 January 2026, asking the court to determine whether Holman's gift was an absolute gift or one that required the council to hold the property on trust. The defendants, David Macklin and Michael Gaye, were the executors of Holman's will. They supported the council's position that the property had been given outright and was not subject to a trust. The hearing took place on 18 June 2026 before HHJ Paul Matthews, sitting as a Judge of the High Court.In considering the case, the judge examined whether Holman's will demonstrated an intention to impose a legally binding trust obligation. He explained that the creation of an express trust requires certainty of intention, subject matter and objects. The use of the word 'trust' is not essential, but the document must demonstrate an intention to impose an obligation on the recipient. The judgment also referred to the established approach that expressions of hope or wishes, without stronger language, do not normally create enforceable trust obligations.The judge found that clause 10(1)(a) required the council to confirm its intention, at the time of accepting the gift, to use the property in accordance with the memorandum. It did not require the council to promise that it would continue doing so indefinitely. HHJ Matthews explained that, had Holman intended to impose a trust, she could have used wording requiring the property to be used exclusively as a museum. Instead, the will required the council to indicate its intention to continue the existing museum without imposing a continuing legal obligation to do so.Why the High Court rejected the possibility of a constructive trustThe judgment also considered whether a constructive trust could arise because the council accepted the property and its subsequent conduct. The judge noted that the council had allowed the property to operate as a museum for more than 40 years, in keeping with Holman's wishes. He therefore found no inequitable conduct that would justify imposing a constructive trust. The possibility of such a trust in circumstances involving different conduct was discussed, but the court did not need to decide that hypothetical question.In his conclusion, HHJ Matthews ruled that the gift was beneficial rather than one made on trust. The judgment stated: "It therefore follows that the claimant has no fiduciary or other duty to preserve the property as a museum for the people of Topsham, or indeed Exeter." He added that the council, as beneficial owner, could depart from Holman's wishes as a matter of property and trust law, although he noted that it had respected those wishes for more than 40 years.The ruling therefore resolved the legal question over ownership and the council's obligations under the will. It established that Exeter City Council was not legally required to preserve 25 The Strand as a museum under a trust, despite Holman's stated wishes for the historic merchant's house.You use AI every day. articles.summary: Hollywood actress Florence Pugh's childhood home is set for a change of ownership, with her parents, Clinton Pugh and Deborah Mackin, putting their
articles.body: Hollywood actress Florence Pugh's childhood home is set for a change of ownership, with her parents, Clinton Pugh and Deborah Mackin, putting their sprawling Oxfordshire property on the market for £1.65 million. The Grade II-listed barn, where the Oppenheimer star spent much of her childhood, holds several family memories and has featured in numerous pictures shared by the actress over the years.According to the Daily Mail, the property, which the couple purchased in October 2011 for £950,000, is now being put up for sale as they reportedly consider downsizing. With Florence and one of her sisters having moved out, the family is understood to be considering a smaller home after years of living in the five-bedroom countryside property.Florence Pugh's childhood home listed for £1.65 millionLocated west of Oxford, the five-bedroom, five-bathroom property is a Grade II-listed former agricultural barn that was converted into a family home. It was listed for sale on September 24 through Knight Frank and other estate agents, with an asking price of £1.65 million.Described on Rightmove as a 'characterful 17th-century barn conversion with a small holding, set within attractive countryside on the edge of Oxford', the property boasts impressive beamed interiors, vaulted ceilings and far-reaching views of the surrounding countryside.The barn also features an annexe and a separate studio, offering additional accommodation and flexible living spaces. The annexe has been particularly useful for the family, as Florence's brother, musician Toby Sebastian, has been living there since they moved into the property.However, Toby recently welcomed a baby with his wife, Scarlet Alexandra, and may now be looking for more space for his growing family.Why Florence Pugh's parents are selling their family homeClinton and Deborah are reportedly considering downsizing after their children gradually moved out of the family home. Florence and one of her sisters have long since left the property, while her younger sister Rafaela, also known as Raffie, is understood to still live there with their parents.Florence has three siblings: vocal coach Arabella Gibbins, 40, musician Toby Sebastian, 34, and Rafaela, 23.In a statement accompanying the property listing, the owners reflected on what made the barn special to them, highlighting its location, spacious interiors and the lifestyle it offered.They said the property had always stood out because of its unique position, offering extensive countryside views while remaining close to Oxford and its amenities.The family also enjoyed maintaining a vegetable garden, keeping chickens and creating an environment that attracted different kinds of wildlife.Describing the interiors, the owners said the barn was 'wonderfully light and spacious', with double-height ceilings adding to the sense of openness in its main living areas.They also highlighted the versatility of the annexe, which offered independent accommodation for family members and guests, complete with its own garden and parking. The separate studio, built during their ownership, could also serve as a home office, hobby room or additional accommodation, subject to the necessary permissions.Reflecting on their years there, they added that the barn had been a wonderful home for bringing family and friends together while enjoying the benefits of countryside living and proximity to Oxford.Florence Pugh has shared several memories from the barnOver the years, Florence has offered glimpses of her family home through social media. In December 2015, she shared a photograph of the Pugh family sitting together on a new sofa in their living room. Recalling the moment, she mentioned that her father had tickled her just as the picture was being taken.Other photographs showed Florence spending time with chicks in the garden, celebrating birthdays and Christmas with her family, and enjoying everyday moments around the house.The actress also shared pictures with Game of Thrones star Maisie Williams in the property's annexe. The two actors had worked together in Florence's film debut, The Falling, in 2014.Some of the family's more personal moments also found their way onto social media, including a photograph of Toby holding the family cat in the barn's kitchen and a video of Florence singing in the annexe.Toby's Instagram posts have also featured the property, including a video of Clinton putting up a Christmas tree inside the barn. More recently, Clinton was photographed in the living areas in April while showcasing his collection of paintings by artist Sacha Jafri, which was set to feature in a charity exhibition.From Oxford childhood to Hollywood stardom: Florence Pugh's journeyFlorence grew up in Oxford, although her family spent a few years in Spain when she was a young child. She moved there at the age of three in the hope that the warmer climate would help with her childhood asthma and tracheomalacia, a condition affecting the windpipe. The family returned to Oxford three years later as her health improved.Her father, Clinton Pugh, has run several restaurants in Oxford and has also been an outspoken critic of the city council's low-traffic policies.Florence, meanwhile, went on to establish herself as one of Hollywood's prominent actors, with performances in films such as Lady Macbeth, Little Women, Black Widow, Oppenheimer and Dune: Part Two.Her recent major project saw her portray Cathy Ames in the Netflix miniseries East of Eden, an adaptation of John Steinbeck's 1952 novel of the same name. Pugh also served as a producer on the series, with critics praising her performance.Ready to Make a Smarter Property Decision? Build Your Legacy with TOI Homes.

articles.title: Daylight saving time 2026 ends in the US: Clocks fall back an hour, and sleep experts aren't happy
articles.summary: Most of the US turned its clocks back by an hour on Sunday, November 1, as daylight saving time ended for 2026.
articles.body: Most of the US turned its clocks back by an hour on Sunday, November 1, as daylight saving time ended for 2026. The switch happened at 2 am local time, the night after Halloween, giving millions an extra hour of sleep and much darker evenings until mid-March.The change comes as President Donald Trump pushes to make daylight saving time permanent. Sleep experts also want to scrap the twice-yearly switch, just not the way the White House does. They prefer permanent standard time, the very clock Americans returned to this weekend.Smartphones update on their own, but ovens, microwaves and car dashboards need a manual reset. Hawaii and most of Arizona skip DST, so their clocks stayed put, as did US territories like Puerto Rico and Guam. The Navajo Nation in Arizona does switch to match its communities in New Mexico and Utah.The difference shows quickly. Boston's sun set at 5:39 pm on Saturday and at 4:37 pm on Sunday, according to the National Weather Service.For Indians, the gap with the US East Coast widens to 10.5 hours from 9.5, and with the West Coast to 13.5 hours from 12.5. The New York Stock Exchange now opens at 8 pm IST instead of 7 pm.Donald Trump's permanent daylight saving time push is stuck in the SenateThe House passed the Sunshine Protection Act with bipartisan support in July. It would keep clocks on DST all year, meaning later winter sunrises and sunsets, while letting states opt out of daylight saving time entirely.The bill has stalled in the Senate, where Arkansas Republican Tom Cotton leads the opposition. In October, Trump accused Cotton of blocking it and posted the senator's cellphone number on social media, urging people to call him. Cotton pointed out that the US had tried permanent DST before and dropped it after people faced "absurdly late sunrises in the winter."That attempt came in 1974, during the energy crisis, and was reversed within a year over concerns about children going to school in the dark.Sleep experts and most Americans would rather keep standard timeThe American Academy of Sleep Medicine backs permanent standard time as it aligns better with the body's natural sleep cycle. Experts warn that darker mornings and brighter evenings can throw off sleep, and permanent DST would send millions of children to school before sunrise.Public opinion leans the same way. A Gallup survey found 48% of Americans favour permanent standard time, against 24% who want permanent DST.Time is also running out for the bill. All pending legislation expires in early January, when lawmakers elected in Tuesday's midterms take office. If it dies, both chambers start over.So for now, the sleep experts have the clock they prefer. That lasts until March 14, 2027, when Americans spring forward again, an unusually late date because March begins on a Monday.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: A Delaware couple cared for a backyard triangle for over 20 years before neighbours demanded $30,000 to let them keep the fenced land; an October 30 court ruling has now awarded the entire disputed strip to the couple
articles.summary: A long-running property dispute between neighbours in Newark, Delaware, has ended with a court ruling that gives homeowners legal ownership of a piece of
articles.body: A long-running property dispute between neighbours in Newark, Delaware, has ended with a court ruling that gives homeowners legal ownership of a piece of land they had looked after for more than 20 years. According to legal documents published by Justia Law, the Delaware Court of Chancery issued a decision in an adverse possession case involving Plaintiffs Joseph W.C. Murray, Jr. and Danielle F. Murray and Defendants Nikola Preradovic, Rade Preradovic, and Zeljka Preradovic. The dispute involved a triangular piece of land along the boundary between two neighbouring homes in New Castle County. The Murrays showed that they had openly, continuously, and exclusively used the enclosed rear part of the disputed land for more than the 20 years required under Delaware law. As a result, the court awarded them full legal ownership of that section.Decades of maintenance establishing continuous controlCourt records show that the Murrays had looked after the fenced section of land for around 25 years. The family put up fences, maintained the garden, and regularly treated the rear area behind their home as part of their own yard. Over the years, the Murrays placed several personal items inside the fenced area. These included a stone retaining wall, garden features, a beehive, and a decorative statue. Photographs and witness statements presented in court showed that these items had remained there over time. This helped confirm that the family had continued to control and use the rear yard without interruption. Under Delaware property laws, anyone claiming land through adverse possession must prove that their use of the property was open, visible, continuous, exclusive, and against the interests of the legal owner for at least 20 years. The court explained that continuous use does not mean someone must be physically present every minute. Instead, they must act like an owner in a way that suits the type of land involved.Failed negotiations and monetary demandsThe legal dispute began after the Preradovic family bought the neighbouring property at 234 South Dilwyn in December 2022. Soon after buying the property, the new owners noticed differences in the boundary lines after land surveys. They asked the Murrays to move or remove the existing fence. During the first discussions, both sides considered officially changing the property boundaries through New Castle County authorities. However, the talks broke down because they could not agree on the financial terms. Court documents show that the new property owners asked the Murrays to pay $30,000 in exchange for signing a deed transfer that would allow them to keep the fenced land. The Murrays refused to pay and claimed they already had rights to the land because they had used it for many years. The disagreement then led to a formal case in the Court of Chancery. At first, the Murrays asked the court to enforce what they said was an agreement to transfer the land. In an earlier decision, Magistrate in Chancery Loren Mitchell found that the claimed sale agreement could not be legally enforced. This was because both sides had not clearly agreed on the exact legal description of the property. The case then moved forward to a full review of the main adverse possession claim.Division of the disputed triangular parcelWhen reviewing the land and its layout, the Court of Chancery divided the disputed triangular area into three separate sections. These were the enclosed rear yard behind the fence, a stone planter area, and an unfenced grass lawn stretching towards the street. The court decided that the Murrays had met all the legal requirements for adverse possession of the rear section enclosed by the fence and retaining wall. The ruling explained that the fence clearly showed that the family was treating the land as their own. This would have been obvious to anyone who owned or lived on the neighbouring property. However, the court rejected the Murrays' claim to the front sections of the triangular plot. These included the planter area and the front grass strip beside the road. The court found that the family had not maintained these areas regularly. There were periods when the grass became overgrown, and other people also had access to the space. The judge ruled that regularly cutting grass along an unfenced front boundary was not enough to prove exclusive control against the legal owner. Such activity did not meet the legal standard needed to take ownership away from someone who already held the deed. As a result, the court officially awarded the Murrays ownership of the enclosed rear yard. However, the Preradovic family kept legal ownership of the outer front lawn.You use AI every day. articles.title: Restoring fighter strength, accelerating Tejas & AMCA projects, boosting triservice synergy my top priorities: New IAF chief Ashutosh Dixit
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: New Indian Air Force chief Air Chief Marshal Ashutosh Dixit, in his first address after taking charge on Sunday, said restoring the sanctioned
articles.body: NEW DELHI: New Indian Air Force chief Air Chief Marshal Ashutosh Dixit, in his first address after taking charge on Sunday, said restoring the sanctioned fighter squadron strength, accelerating indigenous programmes like Light Combat Aircraft ‘Tejas’ and fifth-generation Advanced Medium Combat Aircraft (AMCA), and strengthening tri-services synergy will be his top priorities.“Tejas MklA and lI, AMCA, Indian sensors and Indian weapons are our highest priority. We will fight with Indian solutions, and we will hold them in numbers that meet our operational demands. Our responsibility is to fight and win, but most importantly it is to deter conflict through credible air power,” the 29th IAF chief, an accomplished fighter pilot with over 3,500 flying hours, said on Sunday. He said “restoring” the IAF's combat strength towards the “sanctioned level” will also be his “foremost task”.The new chief arrived at the parade ground in an electric vehicle, in a move reflecting his push for green mobility.Dixit outlined his core focus areas under the acronym VAYU, defining his ‘vision’ as vigilance and operational readiness, ‘aatmanirbharta’ (self-reliance), ‘yukti’ (tactical innovation), and ‘unity’ of effort across the tri-services.As India’s combat squadrons have depleted to 29 from the sanctioned strength of 42, the IAF is desperately seeking to raise the strength of fighters. The IAF is eagerly waiting for the induction of 180 LCA MK1A aircraft, being manufactured by Hindustan Aeronautics Ltd under two contracts. While the Aeronautical Development Agency (ADA) and HAL are working on the LCA Mk 2 variant, the framework for developing AMCA is being finalised. The IAF is also hoping for an early deal with France on 114 Rafale jets.On the current security situation, the new IAF chief said, “Our security environment remains demanding. In addition, the character of war is being reshaped by new technologies and systems like drones, long-range precision weapons, space, cyber, Al and the electromagnetic spectrum. The air force, while transforming into the force that India will need in the next decade, must always be ready to fight and win.”Dixit also lauded his predecessor Air Chief Marshal AP Singh, saying the IAF, under his leadership, displayed what “precise and decisive” air power can achieve during Operation Sindoor. “I thank him for handing over a force in a high state of readiness,” he said.“To the fellow citizens of my motherland, please trust that your Air Force is vigilant, ready and resolute. Our commitment is clear —to remain ready, to keep transforming and to deliver whenever the nation calls,” he said.The IAF chief also underlined his priorities for the welfare of air warriors, Agniveers (Vayu), civilians, veterans, Veer Naris and their families. “Their training, professional excellence, morale, safety, welfare and dignity will have my personal attention.”Before receiving the guard of honour, new Air Chief Marshal Ashutosh Dixit laid a wreath at the National War Memorial (NWM) to honour fallen heroes. Accompanied by family members, he sought blessings of his mother, Nirmala Dixit, and mother-in-law, Kamla Pandey, touching their feet prior to the ceremony.

articles.title: Over 300 arrested outside US Embassy in London amid protests against ban on Palestine Action group
articles.summary: A demonstration outside the US Embassy in London against the UK government's ban on Palestine Action leads to over 300 arrests. Participants rallied for freedom of expression amid claims of repression surrounding the proscription of the group.
articles.body: More than 300 people were arrested during a demonstration outside the US Embassy in London against the UK government's ban on Palestine Action, with police reporting 325 detentions over the weekend.Hundreds gathered in the Nine Elms area on Saturday, holding placards opposing the group's proscription under terrorism legislation. Some signs read: “I oppose genocide, I support Palestine Action.”The Metropolitan Police said on Sunday that 320 of the 325 arrests were made on suspicion of expressing support for a proscribed organisation under the Terrorism Act. Officers continued making arrests into the evening, with demonstrators chanting “Free, free Palestine” as people were taken to police vans.The demonstration was organised as part of a series of protests against the government's decision to proscribe Palestine Action in July 2025. The group has since become the subject of thousands of arrests linked to public expressions of support.Defend Our Juries, which has coordinated protests against the ban, said the latest arrests took the total number of people detained in connection with the group beyond 4,000. It described the figure as “truly dystopian” and criticised the arrests as an attack on freedom of expression.Home Office figures obtained by the BBC showed that 3,630 arrests were made in the year ending June 2026. Adding 134 arrests outside Westminster Magistrates' Court earlier this year and those made on Saturday brings the reported total to 4,089.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: 18 missiles beneath the waves? China's mysterious submarine could give US Navy a Pacific nightmare
articles.summary: China is developing an unconventional underwater missile platform that could add a new dimension to its military threat against US naval forces.
articles.body: China is developing an unconventional underwater missile platform that could add a new dimension to its military threat against US naval forces. A mysterious uncrewed trimaran submarine, currently undergoing trials, is estimated to carry up to 18 missiles, potentially including the YJ-20 hypersonic anti-ship weapon.Its unusual design combines the ability to travel underwater with the firepower of a missile arsenal ship, raising questions about how Beijing could use such platforms to challenge US aircraft carrier strike groups in the Indo-Pacific.According to Naval News, the vessel was identified through satellite imagery and is believed to be undergoing trials at Huludao in China.The submarine features an unconventional three-hull configuration, comprising a central hull and two smaller outrigger hulls positioned towards the rear. The design appears intended to provide stability when the vessel surfaces, particularly when its heavy missile launch tubes are raised into firing position.Naval News reported that the central hull contains two large weapons compartments, with missile tubes arranged in circular clusters and stored horizontally. The vessel is estimated to have at least eight launch tubes, with the total capacity potentially reaching 16–18 if both compartments have identical configurations.Unlike conventional submarines that can launch missiles while submerged, the Chinese platform would have to surface, open the compartment doors and raise its missile tubes vertically before firing. The additional hulls could help maintain stability during this process.Naval News, citing ship-design specialist Dr Rachel Pawling of K39 Consulting, estimates the vessel's submerged displacement at approximately 900 tonnes. Its unusual configuration and limited internal space also suggest that it could be designed to operate without a crew.Naval News identified China's YJ-20 hypersonic anti-ship missile as a possible candidate for the platform, given its large launch compartments and the missile's existing integration with Chinese naval vessels.A subsequent report by Defense Express suggested that the submarine could carry between 16 and 18 YJ-20 missiles, with an estimated range of 1,500–2,000 km and terminal speeds approaching Mach 9 (around 11,000 km/h). The missile is designed to target high-value naval assets, including aircraft carriers and other major warships.How could the submarine launch an attack?The vessel could follow an unconventional operating concept, using underwater movement to approach a designated launch area before surfacing to fire its missiles. Unlike conventional submarines equipped with underwater launch systems, the trimaran would need to expose its missile compartments before raising the launch tubes vertically.The vessel could operate by approaching a designated launch area while remaining submerged before surfacing to deploy its missiles.Its operations may depend on targeting inputs from China's wider military surveillance network, including satellites, reconnaissance aircraft and naval assets, to identify and track moving enemy warships.Once it receives the necessary targeting information, the vessel could surface, raise its missile tubes and launch a coordinated salvo before attempting to submerge and withdraw.Why the development matters for the US NavyThe development could add another layer to China's anti-access/area-denial (A2/AD) strategy, which seeks to restrict the ability of US aircraft carriers and other major warships to operate close to Chinese territory.A mobile underwater missile platform could complicate US efforts to track Chinese launch systems, particularly if multiple such vessels are deployed across the Indo-Pacific.For the US Navy, the potential combination of underwater mobility and a large missile payload presents a different challenge from conventional surface-based launch systems.A vessel capable of carrying 16–18 long-range missiles could potentially launch a concentrated attack against a naval formation, forcing its escorts to deal with multiple incoming threats simultaneously.

articles.title: New Zealand school finance administrator stole $375,000 over seven years by creating, approving and paying 77 fake invoices from a building project’s funds
articles.summary: A school finance administrator in New Zealand stole $375,000 from the school over seven years by creating and paying false invoices from a building
articles.body: A school finance administrator in New Zealand stole $375,000 from the school over seven years by creating and paying false invoices from a building project’s funds. The employee used money allocated for the project to make payments to himself, disguising the documents as invoices from companies that had previously worked for the school. The fraud came to light while the employee was on leave, after an external contractor noticed that project invoices and payments did not match. According to the Serious Fraud Office (SFO), the employee had worked at the school for 20 years before it was uncovered. The employee created, approved, and paid 77 false invoices. None of the services listed had been provided to the school.How the employee used 77 fake invoices to steal school fundsThe employee worked as an internal finance administrator and was responsible for the school’s day-to-day finances. Over seven years, he used funds set aside for a large building project to pay himself through 77 false invoices. The documents were fabricated to make them appear as though they had been issued by companies that had previously carried out work for the school.The employee created, approved and paid the invoices. None of the services recorded in them had been provided to the school. The employee rationalised the conduct by saying he had been underpaid for services provided during his 20 years of employment at the school.An external contractor raised concerns while the employee was on leaveThe fraud was detected while the finance administrator was on leave. An external contractor became suspicious after noticing that invoices and payments connected with the building project did not match. The contractor raised the concerns with the school’s Principal. The school then carried out an internal investigation and uncovered the fraud. It followed due process by reporting the matter to the Ministry of Education, which referred the case to the Serious Fraud Office. The employee was subsequently sent to prison for two years and three months.Seven-year theft left school struggling to fund student resourcesThe SFO recorded a detected financial loss of $375,000 over the seven years. More than 100 hours of employee and volunteer time were also spent on the investigation, involving school staff and members of the Board of Trustees.The school reported that 3,000 students had passed through during the period in which the fraud took place. It said those students were deprived of access to additional resources, including teacher aides, new textbooks, school tablets, sports uniforms and programmes supporting students at risk.The Office of the Auditor General reported that the school was among the top 25 financially struggling schools nationwide and faced serious financial difficulties expected to continue for many years.New framework aims to prevent further misuse of school fundsAfter the fraud was uncovered, the school strengthened its internal processes and controls. It engaged a specialist adviser to develop a new control framework for its financial processes. The case highlighted the importance of separating duties so that one person was not responsible for several parts of a transaction.The case study also identified several warning signs in the employee’s working practices. These included rarely taking leave, not sharing responsibilities, and refusing to delegate tasks to colleagues.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: 'Smoke and mirrors': French students to resume school blockades from Monday
articles.summary: High school blockades in France are set to resume on Monday, November 2, as student groups step up protests against rising prices, inequality and
articles.body: High school blockades in France are set to resume on Monday, November 2, as student groups step up protests against rising prices, inequality and deteriorating education conditions.Pierre Sourzat, head of the student group Lycéens!, said some schools would be blocked when students return from a two-week holiday, with more disruptions expected from Tuesday, according to a report by France 24."It will be more significant from Tuesday, but we know that some schools will be blocked as early as tomorrow," Sourzat told broadcaster RMC on Sunday."We support all our comrades who are blocking their schools from tomorrow," he added.The announcement came a day after hundreds of thousands of people, including high school and university students, took to the streets across France for a third consecutive weekend of protests. Around 320,000 demonstrators participated in largely peaceful rallies on Saturday.Student groups have rejected the government's proposals to address their demands, saying the measures fall short of what they had sought. On Monday, the government announced plans to replace the university admissions platform and provide loans for school renovations.Sabrine Kharbach, spokeswoman for the Union Etudiante (Student Union), said on Saturday that universities and high schools would face blockades on Tuesday and Thursday.French President Emmanuel Macron has urged students to return to classes peacefully, arguing that "young people have been heard".However, Sourzat disagreed, saying "the president hasn't listened to us"."It's smoke and mirrors," he said. "There's a bit of polish on the surface, but once you scratch beneath it, there's nothing there."Sourzat said the proposed overhaul of the university admissions platform, which has faced long-standing criticism over its lack of transparency, did not address the shortage of places in higher education.He also dismissed the government's plan to reduce class sizes, saying it would apply only to 10th-grade classes."We were asking for all year groups," he said.The protest movement initially emerged from weeks of student demonstrations over worsening learning conditions and inequality. It has since grown into a broader campaign against soaring prices.The government faces limited room to offer further concessions as France's economy, the second-largest in the eurozone, stands on the brink of recession. It is also under pressure to rein in public debt.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Punjab chief minister Bhagwant Mann on Sunday alleged that the Shiromani Akali Dal, Congress and BJP had nothing constructive to offer the
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Punjab chief minister Bhagwant Mann on Sunday alleged that the Shiromani Akali Dal, Congress and BJP had nothing constructive to offer the people of the state. He accused his opposition of prioritising political power and personal interests over public welfare.Addressing a gathering in Punjab, Mann said people had witnessed the difference between self-serving politics and development-driven governance. He also expressed confidence that the Aam Aadmi Party (AAP) would get another opportunity to govern the state in 2027.Taking aim at the Akali Dal, Mann alleged that the party had failed to answer for the painful incidents of sacrilege and had been reduced to the Badal family and a handful of close associates. He described the Congress as a "divided house", where leaders were constantly at loggerheads with one another."These political parties are hand in glove with each other, with their sole agenda being to grab power and protect their vested interests," he alleged.Mann said people had trusted his government so far and expressed hope that they would continue to support it. "The people have witnessed the difference between politics driven by personal interests and governance driven by public welfare. They have trusted me so far, and I hope they will continue to repose their faith in me in the future as well," he said.The chief minister also highlighted the government's Mukh Mantri Mawan-Dheeyan Satkar Yojna, under which Rs 1,291 crore was transferred to the bank accounts of more than 37.43 lakh beneficiaries.He said more than 80 lakh women had registered for the scheme as of October 29. The government is working towards its target of covering one crore women, he added.Mann said the scheme had no restrictive household-based conditions and that every eligible woman was entitled to financial assistance. He claimed it would provide Rs 12,000 crore in assistance annually, making it one of the country's most significant initiatives for women's financial empowerment.Expressing confidence in the AAP's prospects, Mann said voters would reject the opposition's campaign and back the government's work."I am confident that the people of Punjab will give a befitting reply to the misleading propaganda of opposition parties by supporting the politics of development, transparency and public welfare," he said.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Three held over pro-Khalistan graffiti at Delhi Metro stations after Diljit concert
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Three people, including a woman, have been arrested for allegedly writing pro-Khalistan slogans at two Delhi Metro stations, police said on
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Three people, including a woman, have been arrested for allegedly writing pro-Khalistan slogans at two Delhi Metro stations, police said on Sunday. The graffiti also carried a message targeting singer Diljit Dosanjh.The arrests come days after Dosanjh performed in the national capital on Friday as part of his Aura India Tour. The singer is scheduled to take the tour to several other cities over the next two months.The graffiti was found at Jahangirpuri and Shastri Nagar Metro stations on October 29 and 30, respectively. Police said the accused were allegedly promised substantial financial rewards for defacing public property at prominent locations in Delhi.The arrested persons have been identified as Sumeet alias Raftar (30), a resident of Panipat in Haryana, and Sumit Kumar alias Kaka (22) and Gurpreet (22), both from Punjab.According to Deputy Commissioner of Police (Special Cell) Narra Chaitanya, the investigation revealed that Sumit Kumar was allegedly the main instigator.Sumeet allegedly painted the slogans near Gate No. 1 of Jahangirpuri Metro station and recorded a video of the act to send to his handlers. Kumar and Gurpreet allegedly defaced a staircase wall near Gate No. 2 of Shastri Nagar Metro station."In both instances, the graffiti read "Diljit Singh quam d gaddar khoon d badla SFJ Khalistan", expressing support for the banned separatist organisation Sikhs For Justice (SFJ) and Khalistan ideology. These acts defaced public property in Metro stations and posed a threat to public order and national integrity," the police said, ANI reported.Police said Sumit Kumar had been in contact with SFJ sympathisers in Ludhiana and Gurdaspur before an associate allegedly instructed him to download an encrypted messaging application.A member linked to the banned separatist organisation Sikhs For Justice (SFJ) allegedly shared graffiti templates through the app and offered him financial rewards for carrying out the activity at prominent Metro stations.Kumar then allegedly recruited Gurpreet and Sumeet to execute the plan. The three travelled to Delhi on October 28, police said.Police said Sumeet ad come in contact with Kumar through online platforms and had visited Ludhiana about a week before the incident. The trio travelled to Delhi by taxi and reached ISBT Kashmere Gate on October 29.Investigators also found that Kumar and Gurpreet had known each other for around four years. Kumar allegedly persuaded her to travel to Delhi on the pretext of shopping before informing her about the plan, police said.Police further alleged that Kumar had painted graffiti near the GTK Bypass, under the jurisdiction of Samaypur Badli police station, on October 30. That incident is being investigated separately.Two FIRs were registered at the Metro Azadpur and Metro NSP police stations under Section 3 of the Delhi Prevention of Defacement of Public Property Act, 2007, and Section 62(2) of the Metro Railway (Operation and Maintenance) Act, 2002."Further investigation is underway to identify other persons involved in the network and establish the role of the handlers behind the alleged operation," the officer said.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Will King Charles apologise for slavery? Antigua speech puts Britain's past in spotlight
articles.summary: King Charles III is set to address the lasting pain caused by the transatlantic slave trade during a speech to Commonwealth leaders in Antigua on Tuesday.
articles.body: King Charles III is set to address the lasting pain caused by the transatlantic slave trade during a speech to Commonwealth leaders in Antigua on Tuesday. His visit and address come as fresh calls grow for Britain to formally apologise for its role in slavery.Buckingham Palace said the King would speak with "unflinching honesty" and "sincere sorrow", although it stopped short of indicating whether he would offer an apology on behalf of the UK.The speech will come during the final leg of the King's nine-day Caribbean tour, at the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (CHOGM). His remarks come amid a shift in the government's position, with Prime Minister Andy Burnham saying he was "open" to the possibility of Britain formally apologising for its role in slavery.Burnham made the comments in an opinion piece for The Guardian on Friday night, describing the transatlantic slave trade as a "brutal and barbaric violation" and saying Britain "must face up to the past". It is understood Buckingham Palace was informed of his remarks in advance. However, the King has not changed his speech in response to the prime minister's comments.A Palace spokesperson said the King "will not shy away from confronting the most shameful aspects of the past during this visit"."You may therefore expect him to address them in his speech with unflinching honesty, sincere sorrow, and respect for the wider discussions that will be taking place between relevant governments on this issue at CHOGM and beyond."The spokesperson also made clear that the King would not comment on the government's position on a formal apology. Royal sources stressed that any decision to apologise or consider reparations rested with the government, not the Palace.The UK has never formally apologised for its role in slavery or offered reparations. Burnham has previously maintained the position of his predecessors and stopped short of supporting compensation payments.However, his latest remarks have drawn a sharp response from Conservative Party leader Kemi Badenoch. She described "endless talk about apologies" as a "distraction" from addressing present-day problems.Speaking to BBC Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg, Badenoch said: "The transatlantic slave trade happened centuries ago. It is time for the Commonwealth to start looking forwards, not endlessly backwards."The King's Caribbean tour has brought Britain's colonial past and its legacy back into focus. During his first stop in the Bahamas, he spoke of the "suffering of the past". In Guyana, he visited the site of the 1823 Demerara Slave Rebellion, where hundreds of enslaved people were killed.The King also visited Independence Park, which marks the site of public executions following the rebellion. Buckingham Palace described the visit as an opportunity for him to learn more about the history of slavery and resistance in the region.The engagements have also focused on environmental issues, opportunities for young people and trade ties with Britain. Queen Camilla, who is accompanying the King in Antigua, attended a church service with him on Sunday ahead of celebrations marking the island's Independence Day.A senior royal aide said the King was accustomed to navigating difficult diplomatic issues during overseas visits."His Majesty is well practised on the diplomatic tightrope," the aide said. "He is up for challenging visits with complex issues and relationships in play. He sees it as his role to 'bat for Britain', the Realms and wider Commonwealth."The King has also been keen to strengthen the Commonwealth, which brings together 56 countries. articles.title: Poland’s top court turns into battleground as Tusk and pro-Trump president clash
articles.summary: Poland’s long-running battle over judicial independence has escalated into a confrontation between prime minister Donald Tusk and president Karol
articles.body: Poland’s long-running battle over judicial independence has escalated into a confrontation between prime minister Donald Tusk and president Karol Nawrocki, after the suspension of the Constitutional Tribunal’s leadership triggered protests and a police deployment outside the court in Warsaw.The latest flashpoint came on Friday, when Judge Anna Korwin-Piotrowska announced the one-month suspension of Tribunal president Bogdan Święczkowski and his deputy, Bartłomiej Sochański, and said she would take charge of the institution. The move followed a dispute over the appointment of new judges, whom Święczkowski had refused to allow to take their seats.Nawrocki, an ally of the nationalist Law and Justice party (PiS) and a vocal supporter of US President Donald Trump, abandoned a visit to Senegal and returned to Warsaw. He described the suspension of the Tribunal’s leadership as a “forcible takeover of a constitutional institution”. PiS leaders also condemned the move, accusing Tusk’s government of attempting a coup.Police were deployed outside the court as hundreds of protesters gathered. Officers said their presence followed concerns about possible threats to judges and staff and risks to public order. Police also reported three arrests after people tried to enter the court complex.Tusk defended his government’s actions, saying it was seeking to restore the rule of law after years of political interference in the judiciary under PiS, which governed Poland for eight years until 2023.“This process is difficult, at times even painful, and requires decisive action. There is no other way,” Tusk said in a post on X on Saturday. In a televised address, he said that “shouting, lies, and brawling cannot be the source of law in Poland”.A decade-long dispute over the judiciaryThe Constitutional Tribunal rules on whether legislation complies with Poland’s constitution, giving control over its composition significant political and legal consequences.The current dispute has roots in 2015, when PiS came to power and challenged judicial appointments made by the outgoing government. Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal subsequently found that only three of five appointments made by the outgoing parliament had a valid legal basis. The incoming PiS majority appointed replacements, including for seats that had already been lawfully filled, while then-president Andrzej Duda refused to swear in the three validly elected judges.During its eight years in office, PiS introduced wider judicial changes that critics said increased political influence over the courts. In 2021, the European Commission warned that the party’s actions posed a “systemic risk to the rule of law in Poland” and froze EU funding over concerns about judicial independence.The European Court of Human Rights ruled in 2021 that the participation of an improperly appointed judge had deprived a company of its right to a tribunal established by law. In December 2025, the European Union’s top court also ruled that Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal did not meet the requirements of an independent court.Tusk returned to office in December 2023 promising to restore judicial independence. But efforts to reverse the changes have been complicated by the continued presence of PiS-appointed judges and Nawrocki’s role in the appointment process.This year, parliament elected eight judges to the Tribunal’s 15-member bench. Nawrocki administered the oath to three but withheld it from five others, who took their oaths without his presence. Święczkowski subsequently refused to allow the five to begin their work.The latest confrontation followed the appointment of Maciej Berek, a former minister in Tusk’s cabinet, who was prevented from taking his seat last week. The choice has also drawn criticism from within the governing camp, with some questioning whether appointing a former government minister is consistent with promises to depoliticise the judiciary.Legal experts have raised questions about the latest intervention, too. Korwin-Piotrowska’s authority to suspend the Tribunal’s president and deputy has been disputed, with her claim based on her length of service as a judge overall rather than seniority within the Tribunal.A standoff with no clear resolutionThe confrontation has exposed a difficult question for Tusk’s government: how to restore the Tribunal’s independence without creating new doubts about the legality of its actions.Marcin Matczak, a Polish lawyer, told Al Jazeera that PiS was seeking to retain control of what he described as its remaining institutional stronghold, while the government wanted to restore balance to the Tribunal. He warned that the use of police in a dispute involving the court could set a precedent for future governments.The US ambassador to Poland, Tom Rose, urged all sides to avoid escalation, warning that large crowds outside the Tribunal could make an already dangerous situation more combustible.The standoff comes as Poland faces security concerns linked to Russia’s war in neighbouring Ukraine and sabotage attacks that Tusk has attributed to Moscow. Tusk has accused his opponents of finding support among pro-Russian forces, an allegation that further sharpens the political divide.With parliamentary elections due next year, the dispute over the Tribunal is likely to remain central to the debate over Poland’s political direction and its relationship with the European Union.You use AI every day. articles.title: US Senator Chris Murphy hospitalised after suffering stroke
articles.summary: US Senator Chris Murphy has been hospitalised after suffering a stroke, his chief of staff told Politico on Sunday, adding that the Connecticut Democrat
articles.body: US Senator Chris Murphy has been hospitalised after suffering a stroke, his chief of staff told Politico on Sunday, adding that the Connecticut Democrat was responding well to treatment and was expected to make a full recovery.Murphy began experiencing numbness in his arm on Saturday afternoon while attending his son's hockey game. He was taken to a local hospital, where doctors diagnosed him with a stroke, before he was transferred to Johns Hopkins for further monitoring, chief of staff Allison Herwitt said in a statement, as reported by Politico."He is awake and alert, and we are optimistic he will make a full recovery," Herwitt said, adding that doctors were encouraged by his progress.The 52-year-old senator had been travelling across the country to campaign for Democratic candidates, with recent visits to Michigan, Minnesota and Florida. He was scheduled to attend campaign events in New Hampshire on Sunday, which are now likely to be affected by his hospitalisation.Murphy's hospitalisation comes days after he made headlines for strongly criticising the Trump administration's reported plans for a fresh military offensive against Iran. Speaking at an event organised by the Middle East Institute in Washington on Wednesday, he described the proposal as "insane", warning that it could trigger a devastating escalation and potentially involve attacks on civilian infrastructure.Murphy, who serves on the Senate Foreign Relations and Appropriations committees, is also viewed as a potential contender for the 2028 Democratic presidential nomination.You use AI every day. articles.summary: Three children aged 3-5 drowned in a pond at Jhadeswar village, Cuttack, while reportedly trying to pluck lily flowers; bodies sent for postmortem.
articles.body: Bhubaneswar: Three children, aged between three and five, drowned while they were reportedly trying to pluck lily flowers from a pond at Jhadeswar village under Bhadreswar police station area in Cuttack district on Sunday.“The deceased belonged to two families. Two of the victims, aged three and five, were siblings, while the third child was four years old,” SP (Cuttack rural) Vinit Agrawal said.According to police sources, the children were playing near their homes before they wandered to the nearby pond. articles.title: Sea turtle season to start with awareness drives
articles.summary: Chennai gears up for Nov–May sea turtle season with fisherfolk awareness drives, 5-nautical-mile trawler buffer, turtle-excluder devices, patrolling and beach cleanups.
articles.body: Chennai: With the sea turtle season (Nov-May) set to start soon, state govt officials are planning to kick-start preparations by holding awareness drives among fishermen to use trawlers cautiously.Forest department officers have been instructed to hold inter-departmental meetings with the fisheries department, coastal security groups, and local bodies this month as part of pre-season activities (Oct to Dec) to prepare for the season. This year, officials plan to go by the book—as the forest department released a standard operating procedure for sea turtle conservation last month, detailing the procedures to be followed by government departments and the public.The turtles will mate during Nov and through half of Dec. Peak nesting happens from the end of Dec through Feb and hatching happens in March. The season spans Nov-May.The awareness will begin with the fisheries department. “We will visit fisherfolk in the coming days and sensitise them to using trawlers cautiously. More precaution needs to be taken during the nesting season from mid Dec, and trawlers must maintain a buffer of 5 nautical miles from the coast to avoid hurting turtles,” an inspector of fisheries said, adding that fishermen will be sensitised to use turtle-excluder devices mandatorily.Coastal security groups will engage in moderate patrolling for about 2-3 hours, and environmental groups will be called in to carry out beach clean up. “Much of the work will begin later this month and in Dec, closer to nesting. articles.title: Two Texas homeowners saw their backyards collapse down an 80-foot creek slope, leaving houses unsafe; after insurers refused payment, an appeals court reopened the fight over whether landslides are covered
articles.summary: A legal dispute over home insurance coverage in Travis County has been sent back to court after a state appeals court ruled that an insurance company must
articles.body: A legal dispute over home insurance coverage in Travis County has been sent back to court after a state appeals court ruled that an insurance company must provide evidence about what caused a major backyard landslide before refusing to pay a claim under its standard policy exclusions. According to legal documents published by Justia Law, the Texas Third Court of Appeal in Austin overturned a trial court's summary judgment in _Privilege Underwriters Reciprocal Exchange v. Michael MacDougall and William Heyer_. The appeals court issued its ruling on 30 October. The decision sends insurer PURE back to court to determine whether human activity helped cause two residential backyards to collapse down an 80-foot slope. The dispute began when the rear sections of neighbouring properties owned by Michael MacDougall and the estate of the late George S. Heyer Jr. suddenly collapsed. Large sections of land broke away and slid down a steep slope towards a local creek. The damage left both homes unsafe, with the buildings sitting dangerously close to the edge of the cliff.Insurer denied claims under standard earth movement exclusionAfter the slope collapsed, MacDougall and the Heyer estate filed insurance claims under their high-end homeowners policies with Privilege Underwriters Reciprocal Exchange (PURE). They asked the insurer to cover structural repairs, work to stabilise the land and other related losses. PURE rejected the claims, pointing to the policy's standard exclusion for earth movement and landslides. The insurer argued that natural movement of the land and damage to the slope caused the collapse. It said the policy clearly excluded this type of damage, even if other factors had also played a role. The homeowners then sued PURE for breach of contract and for failing to pay their claims on time under the Texas Insurance Code. The Travis County 250th District Court granted summary judgment in favour of the homeowners on the question of liability, making the insurer responsible for the loss. PURE later challenged that decision in the appeals court.Appellate court defines scope of landslide exclusionsIn its decision, the Third Court of Appeal considered whether the policy's landslide exclusion also applies when human activity or man-made conditions help cause land to move. The appeals court explained that, under established rules for interpreting insurance contracts, exclusion clauses must be read strictly against the insurance company. The judges found that PURE's policy did not specifically exclude landslides caused by a combination of natural and human-related events. Therefore, the exclusion only applies when natural events alone cause the landslide. The judges also pointed out that some other standard insurance policies clearly exclude earth movement caused by any combination of natural and man-made forces. However, PURE's policy did not contain such wide-ranging wording.Fact issues remain over human causation and site conditionsThe appeals court reviewed expert statements submitted during the earlier court proceedings. These included reports from geotechnical engineers Terrance Zich and Andrew Davidoff. PURE argued that their reports showed that natural environmental conditions were the main cause of the slope collapse. However, the three-judge panel found that the different expert opinions raised an important question that still needed to be answered. There was not enough agreement to determine whether the collapse was caused only by natural erosion or whether human activities also played a part. Possible human causes included construction work, changes to drainage systems and land management activities. Because the exact cause of the land movement remains disputed, the appeals court ruled that neither side was entitled to summary judgment on liability as a matter of law. Lower court judgment reversed for trial proceedingsThe Third Court of Appeal overturned the district court's summary judgment ruling that had held PURE responsible for the loss. It also reversed a related award of statutory interest under the Texas Prompt Payment of Claims Act. The appeals court sent the case back to the 250th District Court of Travis County for further hearings and the presentation of more evidence. The lower court will now examine the facts to establish the exact cause of the landslide.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.
